feedback: If the learner predicts the water will just mix in or float on top, use the observed sinking to revise: denser water sinks beneath lighter water.
If the learner reasons on temperature alone, compare salty vs fresh cold water so salinity's contribution is visible.
Connect back: ask how sea-ice formation makes the leftover water saltier (salt is excluded as ice forms), boosting the sinking.
activities.intendedInsight: Cold, salty water is denser than warm or fresher water, so it sinks beneath them. In the real ocean, this sinking in polar seas is a key physical driver of thermohaline circulation, alongside winds and mixing. Both temperature and salinity matter.
learnerActions: Predict, with a reason, what will happen when cold, salty, dyed water is gently poured into a clear tank of room-temperature plain water (will it mix in, float on top, or sink?).
Pour it in and observe what happens. If the water is salty enough and poured gently, the cold salty water should sink and spread along the bottom as a density current.
Explain how this models polar surface water sinking to drive the global conveyor.
Test a variation: discuss or try cold but FRESH (unsalted) water — would it sink as strongly? Use this to separate the roles of temperature and salinity.
activities.title: Density current demo: cold salty water sinks

feedback: If a learner orders currents before sinking, point back to the driver: sinking comes first and pulls the loop.
If a learner picks warm/salty as densest, compare with cold/salty to show cold adds to density too — cold AND salty is the densest combination.
For the 'slowed conveyor' discussion, accept reasoned answers and probe for the link between sinking and heat transport to distant regions.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can state and order the mechanisms and justify which water sinks (cold/salty is densest), then extend the reasoning to a 'what if the conveyor slowed' case.
learnerActions: Order the stages of the conveyor from polar sinking to warm currents reaching mid-latitudes.
Answer short questions on albedo (bright vs dark surfaces) and density (which water sinks: warm/fresh, warm/salty, cold/fresh, cold/salty).

Discuss with a partner or mentor: if polar sinking slowed or stopped, what might happen to a warm current that helps keep a place like Britain mild — and what's your evidence that polar water really sinks and travels deep?
activities.title: Check and discuss: ordering and density questions
